concepts.title: Conditional Probability from the Joint and the Condition
concepts.definition: Once one event is known to have happened, the chance of another shrinks to the share of the known event's outcomes that also favour the second; it equals the probability of both events together divided by the probability of the known event.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the together-probability by the given event's probability.
question_patterns: find the conditional probability of E given F
evaluate P of A given B from the supplied probabilities
compute the conditional probability when the intersection and the condition are known
what is the chance of the second event knowing the first occurred
determine the probability of a card being even given the number exceeds three
given that at least one child is a boy, find the probability both are boys

solution_steps.action: Divide the joint probability by the condition's probability
solution_steps.explain: P(E given F) = P(E and F) over P(F), valid when P(F) is nonzero.

concepts.title: Properties of Conditional Probability
concepts.definition: Conditioning on a fixed event behaves like rescaling the whole theory: the conditioned chance of the full sample space is one, the conditioned chance of a complement completes it to one, and conditioned unions add with the usual overlap correction.
concepts.formula: P(E_prime given F) = 1 minus P(E given F)
concepts.key_idea: Complement and union rules survive conditioning.
question_patterns: find the conditional probability of the complement of E given F
what is P of S given F for any event F
state the union rule for conditional probabilities
if the conditional chance of E is given, find the conditional chance of not E
prove that conditioning preserves the addition rule for disjoint events
why does the conditioned probability of the whole space equal one

solution_steps.explain: All statements are inside the world where F has occurred.
P(E' given F) = 1 - P(E given F).
P((A union B) given F) = P(A given F) + P(B given F) - P((A intersect B) given F).

concepts.title: Multiplication Rule for Joint Occurrence
concepts.definition: The chance that two events both happen is the chance of the first times the chance of the second given the first; for a chain of events the products keep extending one conditioned factor at a time.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the unconditional first chance by the conditioned second chance.
question_patterns: find the probability that both events occur using the multiplication rule

multiply the first probability by the conditional probability to get the joint one
determine the probability of three specified draws in succession

solution_steps.action: Multiply the first probability by the conditioned second
solution_steps.explain: P(E and F) = P(E) times P(F given E).

concepts.title: At Least One of Two Independent Events
concepts.definition: For two unrelated events, the chance that at least one occurs is one minus the product of their individual miss chances, since both miss only when each fails on its own.
concepts.key_idea: One minus the product of the two failure chances.
concepts.textbook_ref: lemh207.txt example 14 with exercise 13.2 Q12, Q14 (lines ~1049-1059, 1132-1147)
question_patterns: find the probability that at least one of the two events occurs
what is the chance the problem is solved when either person may solve it

find the chance of getting the wanted outcome at least once in two throws

determine the probability that at least one odd number appears

solution_steps.explain: Subtract each event's probability from one.
Subtract the second event's probability from one.
At least one occurs unless both miss, so subtract the product from one.

concepts.title: Testing Independent Events
concepts.definition: Two events are independent exactly when their together-probability equals the product of their separate probabilities, equivalently when conditioning changes nothing; independence differs from mutual exclusivity, which forbids shared outcomes.
concepts.formula: events are independent when P(E and F) = P(E) times P(F)
concepts.key_idea: Compare the joint probability with the product of the separate ones.
question_patterns: check whether the two events are independent

solution_steps.explain: Find P(E) and P(F) from the sample space.
Find P(E and F).
Equality certifies independence; any gap means the events are dependent.

concepts.title: Partition of a Sample Space
concepts.definition: A partition is a family of events that are pairwise disjoint, together cover the whole sample space, and each carry positive probability; an event paired with its complement is the simplest two-piece example.
concepts.formula: a partition is pairwise disjoint, exhaustive and has nonzero probabilities
concepts.key_idea: Exactly one member of a partition occurs in every trial.
question_patterns: show that the given events form a partition of the sample space
what three conditions define a partition of a sample space
explain why an event and its complement partition the sample space
is the collection of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events a partition
verify that the listed hypothesis events are disjoint and exhaustive
give an example of a partition with three members

solution_steps.explain: Members must not share outcomes.
The union of the members must be the whole sample space.
Every member needs a nonzero chance of occurring.

concepts.title: Theorem of Total Probability
concepts.definition: When the causes partition the sample space, the overall chance of an effect is the sum over causes of each cause's probability times the effect's chance given that cause.
concepts.key_idea: Blend the per-cause chances weighted by the prior chances.
question_patterns: find the total probability of the event by weighting each cause's conditional chance
compute the overall chance the job finishes on time with or without a strike
what is P of A by the theorem of total probability
blend the two conditional chances with their prior weights
determine the overall probability of the effect when either cause may act
sum the weighted conditional probabilities over all the causes

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the first prior by the conditional chance under that cause.
Multiply the second prior by the conditional chance under that cause.
The sum is the total probability of the effect.

concepts.title: Bayes' Theorem Reverse Probability
concepts.definition: Bayes' rule flips the conditioning: after an effect is observed, each cause's revised chance is its prior times the effect's chance under that cause, divided by the same product summed over all causes.
concepts.key_idea: Share of the observed effect's weight that belongs to the cause.
question_patterns: given the ball drawn is red, find the probability it came from the second bag
given the item is defective, what is the probability machine B made it
find the probability the person actually has the disease after a positive test
what is the revised chance of the cause after the effect is observed
apply Bayes' theorem to find the posterior probability of the hypothesis
determine which bag the drawn ball most likely came from

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the first prior by the conditional chance of the effect under it.
Add the second prior times its conditional chance; this is the total chance of the effect.
Divide its weight by the total to get the posterior probability.

concepts.title: Random Variable on a Sample Space
concepts.definition: A random variable is a real number assigned to every outcome of a random experiment, such as counting the heads in two tosses; several different random variables can live on the same sample space.
concepts.formula: a random variable maps each outcome of the sample space to a real number
